facts.statement: Junggarsuchus lived during the Late Jurassic period, between 163.5 and 162.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic~163.5 to 162.2 Ma -

facts.statement: The genus Junggarsuchus was described by Clark and colleagues in 2004.
facts.quote: authority: Clark et al., 2004

facts.statement: The name Junggarsuchus is derived from the Junggar Basin where it was found and the Greek word for crocodile.
facts.quote: The generic name of Junggarsuchus comes from the Junggar Basin (the anglicization of Dzungar), where the fossil was found, and the Greek word "souchos" meaning crocodile.

facts.statement: The species name sloani honors C. Sloan, who discovered the holotype specimen.
facts.quote: The specific name, "sloani" is in honor of C. Sloan, who is credited with finding the holotype.

facts.statement: Fossils of Junggarsuchus were found at the Wucaiwan locality in the Shishugou Formation in Xinjiang, China.
facts.quote: Junggarsuchus was found in the upper part of the Lower Member of the Shishugou Formation in Xinjiang, China at the Wucaiwan locality.

facts.statement: The type specimen was initially described in the journal Nature in 2004 by James Clark, Xu Xing, Catherine Forester, and Yuan Wang.
facts.quote: The type and only specimen was described in 2004 by James Clark, Xu Xing, Catherine Forester, and Yuan Wang in Nature

facts.statement: A full osteological description of the specimen was published in 2022 by Alexander Ruebenstahl, Michael Klein, Yi Hongyu, James Clark, and Xu Xing.
facts.quote: it did not receive a full osteological description until 2022 when Alexander Ruebenstahl, Michael Klein, and Yi Hongyu published a monograph along with two of the original describers James Clark and Xu Xing.

facts.statement: The skull of the holotype specimen measures 144 mm in length.
facts.quote: It is a relatively small animal, with the skull of the holotype only measuring 144 mm in length.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus was likely about the size of a domestic cat in life.
facts.quote: This would make the animal in life only about the size of a domestic cat.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen IVPP 14010 includes an almost complete skull, lower jaws, parts of the forelimbs, fifteen vertebrae, and most of the ribcage.
facts.quote: The holotype, given the designation IVPP 14010, consists of an almost complete skull with an intact brain-case and lower jaws, most of the left forelimb, the proximal ends of the ulna and radius of the right forelimb along with the right humerus, fifteen cervical and dorsal vertebrae along with most of the ribcage, and an associated caudal vertebra.

facts.statement: The holotype skull was moved from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology to George Washington University for study using CT imaging.
facts.quote: The skull of the holotype was transported from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, where it was initially reposited, to George Washington University, where it was studied and comprehensively re-described by Ruebenstahl and colleagues using modern CT imaging technology.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus had very little cranial kinesis and powerful jaw muscle attachment sites, traits similar to modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: In their initial description of the skull, Clark and colleagues noted that there was very little cranial kinesis and there were attachment sites for very powerful jaw muscles, which are derived traits found in modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus was adapted for terrestrial locomotion, unlike the semi-aquatic movement of modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: As in other sphenosuchians, the limbs of Junggarsuchus were adapted to terrestrial locomotion (movement on land), rather than the semi-aquatic locomotion seen in living crocodilians.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus possessed a vertically oriented upper arm bone, a ball-and-socket shoulder joint, and a three-fingered hand.
facts.quote: These adaptations include: a vertically orientated upper arm bone, ball-and-socket shoulder joint, and a functionally tridactyl (three-fingered) hand due to a reduction of digit 5 and the absence of digit 1.

facts.statement: The lateral surface of the angular bone in Junggarsuchus has extensive jaw muscle attachment sites similar to crown crocodilians.
facts.quote: The lateral surface of the angular bone has extensive attachment sites for jaw musculature, which is seen in some crown crocodilians, but not in other intermediate forms.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus had a tall and narrow semicircular canal in its inner ear, an adaptation believed to aid in head orientation and gaze while on land.
facts.quote: Notably, the inner ear anatomy of Junggarsuchus shows significant terrestrial adaptations. The semicircular canal is tall and narrow, unlike in aquatic crocodilians, which is believed to have aided the animal in the orientation of the head and the gaze.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the lack of osteoderms in Junggarsuchus is due to taphonomic conditions or because the specimen was a juvenile.
facts.quote: They suggest that the lack of preserved osteoderms may be a product of the taphonomic conditions of the specimen, or that it may have been a juvenile when it died.

facts.statement: The function of pneumatic spaces in the Junggarsuchus skull is debated; they may absorb shock or result from cranial sinus invasion.
facts.quote: However, the authors note that this is only inferred, and the evolution of cranial pneumaticity in crocodylomorphs may instead reflect the invasion of these tissues by cranial sinuses.

facts.statement: The exact contact between the surangular and angular bones in Junggarsuchus is uncertain, with possibilities ranging from short contact to significant contact similar to Dibothrosuchus.
facts.quote: However, it is possible that the surangular has significant contact across a significant length of both the articular and angular bones, which would make it similar to the condition of its close relative Dibothrosuchus.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus had only three digits in contact with the ground in its forelimbs, a reduction from the ancestral five digits seen in pseudosuchians.
facts.quote: These include the reduction of the number of digits in contact with the ground from five, which is the ancestral condition in pseudosuchians, to only three in the forelimbs of Junggarsuchus.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus possessed an enlarged surface on the front edge of its shoulder blade, likely for expanded muscle attachments to help retract its limbs.
facts.quote: Other limb specializations include an enlarged surface on the anterior edge of the scapula, which has been interpreted as a site for expanded muscle attachments to aid in limb retraction.

facts.statement: The shoulder and limb joints of Junggarsuchus were oriented to hold its limbs directly underneath its body, allowing them to flex beneath it.
facts.quote: The joints of the shoulders and limb bones also appear to be generally oriented in such a way that the limbs would be held directly underneath the body and would have the ability to flex underneath the body of the animal.

facts.statement: Later authors suggest Junggarsuchus genuinely lacked osteoderms, reflecting a trend toward terrestrial mobility and flexibility not seen in modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: The notable lack of osteoderms which, in the original description, was suggested to be purely taphonomic, is suggested by later authors to be reflective of a genuine lack of these features as part of a general trend towards more terrestrial mobility and flexibility which is not seen in the modern relatives of Junggarsuchus.

facts.statement: Spinal characteristics in Junggarsuchus suggest a much more flexible range of motion than that found in most modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: Characteristics of the spine including the zygapophyses are suggestive of a much more flexible overall range of motion that most modern crocodiles lack completely.

facts.statement: James A. Clark and colleagues originally described Junggarsuchus as the sister taxon to the clade Crocodyliformes.
facts.quote: The original description of Junggarsuchus by James A. Clark and colleagues found it to be the sister taxon to the clade Crocodyliformes

facts.statement: Some analyses found Phyllodontosuchus to be the sister taxon to Junggarsuchus, but this relationship was weakly supported due to the poor preservation of Phyllodontosuchus.
facts.quote: Phyllodontosuchus was also found to be the sister taxon to Junggarsuchus, although this was weakly supported because Phyllodontosuchus is only known from a single, heavily deformed skull and associated teeth, and its placement in the authors' phylogeny varied considerably in regard to its affinities.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus is from the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: The three taxa that define Solidocrania, Junggarsuchus, Macelognathus, and Almadasuchus, are all Late Jurassic in age

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus was among the earliest-diverging crocodylomorphs to possess a linear arrangement of foramina below the lower jaw teeth.
facts.quote: One of their findings was that Junggarsuchus was among the earliest-diverging crocodylomorphs to have a linear arrangement of foramina below the teeth of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus had a much lower density of facial nerves along its snout compared to comparable taxa like Macelognathus and Litargosuchus.
facts.quote: Junggarsuchus is a notable outlier in this trend because the inferred density of these nerves is much lower than in comparable taxa such as Macelognathus and Litargosuchus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Solidocrania is a natural clade or if its defining skull traits resulted from convergent evolution rather than shared ancestry.
facts.quote: However, the authors are careful to note that, given the late appearance of Junggarsuchus and other basal solidocranian taxa, it is possible that Solidocrania is not a natural clade and that the uniting skull characteristics could be a secondarily derived trait that is a result of convergent evolution rather than traits inherited from a shared common ancestor with crocodyliformes.

facts.statement: Researchers believe Junggarsuchus was almost certainly carnivorous, similar to most other crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: Junggarsuchus was almost certainly carnivorous, like most other crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus possessed xiphodont teeth with serrations adapted for cutting flesh.
facts.quote: It possessed xiphodont teeth with serrations which were adapted for cutting through flesh.

facts.statement: Indirect evidence suggests Junggarsuchus likely fed on small animals such as primitive mammals, squamates, and possibly hatchling dinosaurs.
facts.quote: the Junggarsuchus most likely fed on small animals like primitive mammals, squamates, and possibly hatchling dinosaurs.

facts.statement: The only known remains of Junggarsuchus were discovered near the town of Wucaiwan in Xinjiang, China.
facts.quote: The only remains of Junggarsuchus so far described were discovered near the town of Wucaiwan in Xinjiang, China.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus fossils come from the lower member of the Shishugou Formation, dating from 164 to 159 million years ago.
facts.quote: This locality is a part of the lower member of the Shishugou Formation, which ranges from 164 to 159 million years ago.

facts.statement: The specific layer containing Junggarsuchus fossils is believed to represent traditional fluvial or wetland environments with less intense flooding.
facts.quote: The upper portions of this member, where Junggarsuchus was found, are believed to have consisted of more traditional fluvial or wetland environments with less-intense flooding than the lower portions of the member.

facts.statement: The genus Junggarsuchus was described by Clark et al. in 2004.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Clark et al., 2004

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Junggarsuchus is J. sloani, described by Clark et al. in 2004.
facts.quote: subdivision: * J. sloani Clark et al., 2004 (especie tipo)

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus is an extinct genus of sphenosuchian crocodylomorph from the Middle Jurassic of China.
facts.quote: Junggarsuchus es un género extinto de crocodilomorfo esfenosuquio del Jurásico Medio de China.

facts.statement: Like other sphenosuchians, Junggarsuchus had limbs well adapted for terrestrial movement rather than the semi-aquatic locomotion seen in modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: Igual que en otros esfenosuquios, las extremidades de Junggarsuchus estaban bien adaptadas para el desplazamiento terrestre, más que al estilo de locomoción semiacuática vista en los modernos crocodilianos.

facts.statement: Junggarsuchus adaptations included a vertically oriented humerus, a shoulder joint with a spherical cavity, and a functionally three-toed hand where only three toes touched the ground.
facts.quote: Estas adaptaciones incluyen: un húmero verticalmente orientado, una articulación en el hombro dotada de una cavidad esférica, y una mano funcionalmente tridáctila (solo tres de los dedos se apoyaban en el suelo).

facts.statement: The time range for Junggarsuchus is the Callovian stage, from 165.3 to 161.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Callovian to Callovian (165.3 to 161.5 million years ago)
